items.question: How would you improve hybrid attention to let context windows scale further?
items.object: Replacing global attention with sparse attention in hybrid architectures
items.answer: I think whenever people care about Linear Attention, it is definitely because they have run into some context wall. First, let’s see whether we can get rid of global attention altogether. Yes, that is the first point, because it really is a major bottleneck preventing the context window from continuing to scale up. I think the best way to combine them would be to replace the global attention in hybrid attention with sparse attention. Theoretically, as long as sparse attention can select accurately, it can fully replace the full-attention layer.

items.question: How has your approach to improving linear-attention architectures evolved?
items.object: Research on efficient linear-attention architectures
items.answer: For linear attention, at the beginning I read a lot from a Stanford research group called Hayseed Research—following Albert and the lab he was in at Stanford. I read a lot of their blog posts and felt that sequence modeling was a very interesting problem, so I decided to work on sequence-modeling problems. When I had just started my PhD, Microsoft Research Asia had a piece of work called RetNet. At the time, the initial goal was to improve RetNet’s efficiency and performance. Later, I found that this set of hardware-optimization algorithms for improving efficiency could be extended to many other similar architectures. Subsequent work was mainly about finding ways to further improve the performance of linear-attention architectures while still allowing hardware-efficient training. For example, this went from gating mechanisms to a mechanism called the Delta Rule. Later, we combined those two things into a unified rule and turned it into an RNN update rule. At the same time, there were hardware-efficient algorithms for training it.

items.question: How do you explain what makes linear attention computationally linear compared with ordinary softmax attention?
items.object: Linear attention and its computational complexity relative to softmax attention
items.answer: By linear, we mainly mean linear complexity. Linear complexity is contrasted with quadratic complexity. Ordinary softmax attention has quadratic complexity. As we all know, softmax attention has three matrices: Q, K, and V—query, key, and value. Usually, Q and K are first multiplied to obtain an L-by-L matrix, where L is the sequence length. Then we apply masking to that L-by-L matrix. Since this is basically autoregressive language modeling, we mask out future information. This gives us a lower-triangular L-by-L matrix. We then apply softmax, producing a matrix of attention scores, and finally multiply that attention-score matrix by the value matrix to get an output. That is a very rough introduction to softmax attention in autoregressive modeling. Because it has an L-by-L matrix, its complexity is quadratic. Linear attention generally removes the softmax operator. Once we remove that nonlinearity, softmax, through some algebraic transformations we can write it as something resembling an RNN inference form. Then the cost of each step is O(1), and the total complexity of processing a sequence of length L is O(L). So its complexity scales linearly with length, which is why people call it linear attention.

items.question: How do you place linear attention within the broader landscape of large-language-model research?
items.object: Linear attention within large-language-model architecture research
items.answer: I think it is all modification within the basic Transformer architecture. The LLM technology stack can be divided into pre-training, post-training, and so on. This architecture research is definitely within pre-training. Pre-training has many other research categories too, such as optimizers, fundamental architectures, pre-training data, and so on. Linear attention belongs to research on fundamental architectures. At present, the overall framework of fundamental architectures is still essentially the Transformer: it has an attention mechanism and a feedforward network, and those two modules are repeatedly stacked many times to form the Transformer architecture we know today. Generally, people modify things within this framework. In recent years, people have replaced the traditional MLP, or feedforward network, with mixture-of-experts, or MoE, modules. Linear attention replaces traditional softmax attention with attention mechanisms of linear complexity. Of course, the more popular recent class is hybrid architectures: some layers remain softmax-attention layers, while most other layers are replaced with linear-attention layers.

items.question: Why did you see hybrid attention as a worthwhile direction for Kimi’s long-chain-of-thought reasoning models?
items.object: Kimi’s decision to explore hybrid attention for long-chain-of-thought reasoning
items.answer: At the beginning of the year, the broader backdrop was that DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi 1.5 had just been released. Their core approach involved doing some RL and generating very long chains of thought. They use these very long chains of thought for time scaling, to solve more complex problems. These chains of thought can often reach tens of thousands of tokens. As I understood it, Kimi felt that if every layer used quadratic attention, decoding would become too expensive. First, every layer has to store a large KV cache. In addition, each step has linear time complexity, so if you decode L tokens, the time complexity is also quadratic. So in the context of generating these long chains of thought, Kimi felt it was necessary to invest resources in exploring hybrid attention, because it can substantially lower inference cost. I see this as very useful both in the context of long-chain-of-thought reasoning and in this year’s broader agentic-AI context.

items.question: How do you understand the design of Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) relative to your earlier Gated DeltaNet?
items.object: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) and its finer-grained gating
items.answer: This linear-attention module is basically based on a piece of work I did last year called Gated DeltaNet, with some improvements made on top of it, eventually forming KDA. Broadly speaking, first we have something called the Delta Rule, which we can discuss in more detail later. In Gated DeltaNet, that work was constrained by efficiency, so I used scalar-value gating similar to Mamba2. This means that for an attention head, all dimensions under it share a single decay rate. That creates some computational simplification. So at the time, the consideration was: first add the Delta Rule on the basis of Mamba2, while ensuring efficiency. Therefore, we only used that coarser-grained gating mechanism. That is Gated DeltaNet. KDA, which Zhang Yu worked on, replaces this coarser-grained decay rate with a finer-grained one. Previously, different dimensions within an attention head had to share the same decay rate. Now, each dimension has its own decay rate. As a result, the hidden state of the corresponding RNN memory for each dimension has its own independent update frequency. Intuitively, this can make better use of the RNN’s limited hidden state and improve performance.

items.question: How do you understand the design logic behind Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)?

items.answer: I feel that KDA essentially combines the ideas from my two earlier works. Another earlier work of mine, called Gated Linear Attention, had a finer-grained decay rate. items.question: How do you understand the trade-off between Kimi’s hybrid linear attention and DeepSeek’s sparse attention for long-text decoding?
items.object: Kimi’s hybrid linear attention versus DeepSeek’s sparse attention
items.answer:
I see these two kinds of attention as actually trying to solve the same problem: how to address efficiency in long-text decoding. Kimi is taking the hybrid-attention route. DeepSeek, meanwhile, mainly likes the sparse-attention route. They believe sparsity may be a better way to lower decoding cost.

DeepSeek’s sparse attention apparently does not have full attention. Every layer should be DeepSeek sparse attention. But every layer still has to store the entire KV cache. It can only start from a checkpoint and, through some transformations, obtain something called an index to select top-k tokens. That is DeepSeek’s attention.

On the hybrid-attention route, there are still some global-attention layers, while the faster layers are linear-attention layers. Its benefit is that it can save a lot of KV cache. Hybrid attention not only reduces KV cache—it can reduce a great deal of KV cache, because most layers are RNN-like layers—it also improves decoding efficiency. Since the KV-cache size is reduced, larger batch sizes may be used during decoding; previously they may not have fit, but with KV cache greatly reduced, batch size can perhaps be increased. DeepSeek sparse attention does not reduce KV cache, but it can reduce the cost of generating each token through sparse activation.

items.question: How do you interpret MiniMax’s decision to return to full attention in M2?
items.object: MiniMax M2’s return to full attention
items.answer: I think the team responsible there is very open, and they shared a lot of experience. I think that experience is very valuable. For example, as I recall, they said that for their first version, the metrics they monitored showed that the Lightning Attention module they used performed very well on those metrics. Since that linear attention was also more efficient, they ultimately chose it. Later they found that on tasks such as multi-hop reasoning, the performance drop was very large. The original plan was chosen because they had not initially tested multi-hop reasoning ability; they mainly looked at capabilities such as MMLU. In my view, the linear attention they selected was actually a relatively weak one. Linear attention has developed a lot in the past two years, but the one they used felt like linear attention from two years ago, with the technology still at that point. It is quite possible that their first-version evaluation pipeline was not sufficiently thorough, so they chose a somewhat naïve solution. Recently, they may want to do agentic tasks and coding. Multi-hop reasoning becomes very important in those settings. They found the performance gap between linear attention and full attention was still quite large, so for now they went back to a full-attention architecture composed entirely of softmax attention. But they said they are still exploring hybrid-attention architectures, so perhaps the next M3 version will become hybrid attention again.

items.question: How do you understand the role of forgetting mechanisms in the improvement of linear attention?
items.object: The development of forgetting mechanisms in linear attention
items.answer: At the very beginning, I think linear attention simply did not work. It did not work even on short texts. The earliest linear attention was invented around 2020. I think in the intervening years it did not perform very well on language modeling. A more representative later work was ReLA. By adding a forgetting-decay mechanism, it found that linear attention could still achieve relatively good language-modeling performance when scaled up. ReLA added an input-independent decay. An input-independent decay means its forgetting rate is unrelated to the input. For example, if its forgetting rate is 0.99, then after every token, the preceding hidden state is multiplied by 0.99. In this way it forgets one percent of that information, then writes in the new information. This is called input-independent decay, and it is the technique used by ReLA. Later, this kind of input-independent forgetting was gradually replaced by input-dependent decay. For example, as mentioned earlier, my work Gated Linear Attention added a gating mechanism. Mamba and Mamba2 are also closely related to linear attention. Mamba2 in particular can basically be regarded as linear attention with a decay. Its decay is very similar to ReLA’s, except it is determined by input: each token can have a different decay rate. For instance, when it encounters certain tokens and thinks prior content need not be forgotten, it can set the decay rate to 1, so there is no decay of preceding content at all. If it encounters tokens that make it think previous information is no longer useful, it can set the decay to 0 at that position, completely forgetting the preceding state. Since it is multiplied by zero, the preceding state is entirely gone. This kind of input-dependent decay is more flexible: it can learn dynamically from data when to forget and when to retain the preceding state. That was the first major improvement: changing decay from input-independent to input-dependent.

items.question: What do you see as the key improvement the Delta Rule brings to linear attention?
items.object: The Delta Rule as an improvement to linear attention
items.answer: The Delta route changes the update formula from the simple original rule. What Linear Attention uses should be called the Hebbian Rule. This rule simply adds the outer product of key and value to the hidden state. That is a Hebbian rule. The Delta family of models uses something called the Delta Rule. With the Delta Rule, at each step, it first uses the key to retrieve from memory, returning a value: the value that key originally corresponds to in memory, which we call the old value. The key also has an input value, which we call the input value. From the perspective of an associative-memory network, we want each key to correspond to only one value. But the model does not know whether it should correspond to the previous value or the input value. So we have a learnable term called beta. We can view beta as a coefficient between 0 and 1 that determines how much of the preceding old value and how much of the input value to use. We make a linear combination using that coefficient, obtaining the final new value. items.question: How do you explain the recurring waves of interest in Linear Attention?
items.object: Recurring interest in Linear Attention
items.answer: I think whenever people pay attention to Linear Attention, it is because they have hit some context wall. When people first studied Linear Attention, around 2020, it was because they encountered the first context wall. They had hit that wall. If they wanted to continue increasing context, they had to find something with complexity lower than softmax, lower than quadratic. At the time, BERT trained at 512. In that era, people may have considered 2,048—and perhaps 8,192—as long text, because things became very slow there. Later, the birth of Flash Attention broke through that wall. Looking back now, 8,192 is a very short text, and training at that length carries no pressure at all. But before Flash Attention, computation required materializing the quadratic attention matrix in global memory, then moving it from global memory back into flash memory. The resulting memory reads and writes created an enormous overall overhead. And because the attention matrix was materialized in global memory, it could cause out-of-memory problems. That was the original motivation for studying Linear Attention. With Flash Attention, people realized that this wall had in fact been broken: if we can compute softmax attention exactly in this way, there is no need to find linear attention to approximate it. So Linear Attention research became less of a focus. But recently, long-text decoding has once again become a highly demanded capability. Large language models have to emit huge numbers of tokens and perform decoding, and this cost has naturally led people to reexamine this technology. This technology itself has also had years of development in academia. Especially after Flash Attention, academia realized that hardware efficiency was crucial if the Linear Attention family of models was to be accepted. That is why I started a project called Flash Linear Attention: it is devoted to taking these Linear Attention variants, writing a library in Triton and many kernels, so they can run quickly on modern hardware, primarily GPUs. Whenever softmax efficiency becomes a bottleneck, people return to look at Linear Attention. That is roughly the history.

items.question: How do you assess the current consensus around linear attention as an architecture for long-text tasks?
items.object: Pure linear attention and hybrid attention
items.answer: I think the current consensus around Linear Attention is that pure Linear Attention does not work. It has some fairly fundamental shortcomings on long texts. Nowadays, people generally do not try purely linear models. As for more compromise solutions, such as hybrid attention, they still have many linear-attention layers, but they also retain a certain number of global-attention layers. In that way, the model has a guaranteed floor, and it has some guarantee for processing long texts, because it ultimately still has many global-attention layers. A fully linear network may theoretically be unable to perform long-text tasks because its number of RNN states is fixed. As context length increases, sooner or later it cannot store everything, and it will eventually lose a great deal of accuracy. But hybrid attention has many global-attention layers, so it can still complete long-text tasks through them. For example, the Kimi Linear paper and the previous Qwen3 Next showed no degradation on long-text benchmarks such as RULER and other tasks, so it still has a certain degree of long-text capability. Hybrid attention therefore receives a lot of attention. But I do not know whether it counts as a consensus, because different places are still trying different approaches. For example, DeepSeek is trying sparse attention.

items.question: Why do you think a three-to-one ratio of Linear Attention layers to full-attention layers has become the preferred choice for hybrid architectures?
items.object: The three-to-one ratio of Linear Attention layers to full-attention layers in hybrid architectures
items.answer: I think three-to-one is now almost becoming a consensus. MiniMax previously used a seven-to-one ratio. With seven-to-one, there may not have been enough softmax-attention layers, so the guarantee for long text may not have been as strong. I remember that Ziji also released a paper studying hybrid architectures and how much softmax attention they need. They did many pre-training-from-scratch experiments, changing different Linear Attention modules as well as the hybrid ratio. Their conclusion was roughly that a three-to-one ratio was best, and that Gated Attention was better than the other candidates. Later, Qwen3 Next also used three-to-one and the Gated Attention approach. Different vendors that explored it seem to have concluded that this ratio is better. MiniMax may initially not have validated things thoroughly enough. As we said before, its early evaluation may have had some shortcomings, so it used a more aggressive seven-to-one approach. Now things have basically returned to three-to-one. I think three-to-one is a consensus within the otherwise non-consensus area of hybrid linear attention: people use a three-to-one ratio to mix the model.

items.question: How do you think about the trade-off between global-attention layers and linear layers when designing a hybrid architecture?
items.object: The trade-off between global-attention layers and linear layers in hybrid architectures
items.answer: I think there are trade-offs. If there are too few global-attention layers, tasks such as reasoning and long-text tasks will definitely be affected more strongly. There may be no effect on some short-context tasks, such as MMLU. But long-text and reasoning tasks should show a relatively large decline. On the other hand, it is not that more attention layers are always better. After training, people find that most attention layers may not be useful. Only attention in some key layers is useful; not every attention layer is useful. The network itself contains redundancy, which gives us an opportunity to replace some layers with linear layers. So a hybrid architecture does not necessarily mean that it is worse than global attention. It may well be a better replacement overall.

items.question: How do you assess hybrid attention’s current weakness on multi-hop reasoning and its prospects for improvement?
items.object: Hybrid attention’s limitations on multi-hop reasoning and its potential for improvement
items.answer: MiniMax previously released something saying—and I think it was very good that they acknowledged this—that hybrid linear attention, or hybrid sliding-window attention, has shortcomings on long-text multi-hop reasoning. I think that is probably hybrid attention’s only current issue. As far as I know, on other tasks it is basically not worse than an all-softmax-attention model. It only performs worse in multi-hop reasoning, which is fairly understandable: multi-hop reasoning relies heavily on relationships between tokens, and so may rely heavily on the number of softmax-attention layers. There are probably not many tasks that depend heavily on the number of global-attention layers. Perhaps only multi-hop reasoning and long-text reasoning depend on it somewhat; many other tasks basically do not, and so are completely unaffected. If we develop hardware-efficient RNNs with stronger expressive power, the gap on multi-hop reasoning could be directly narrowed and might even be surpassed. For example, in Kimi’s recent Linear work, Zhang Yu found that changing coarse-grained decay to fine-grained decay produced quite considerable improvements on multi-hop reasoning, coding, and math tasks. So hybrid approaches can do better on these tasks. I think hybrid linear attention is only a beginning. Overall, it is quite possible to make better hybrid-attention mechanisms by refining the linear-attention module.

items.object: Songlin Yang’s algorithmic contribution to Kimi’s fine-grained decay work
items.answer: Zhang Yu wanted to experiment with fine-grained decay, so I helped him devise a transformed algorithm for it. items.question: How do you think attention architectures should be improved?
items.object: Attention architecture design
items.answer: I think there are currently only two relatively mainstream routes: hybrid linear and sparse. I think both are very promising. There may also be some less-mainstream attention designs. For example, I saw Meta release a paper last time that did cubic attention: apparently quadratic complexity was not enough, so it went for cubic complexity. Some places also have interesting variants of quadratic-complexity attention. For example, ByteDance previously had one called Deltaformer, which essentially brings the Delta Rule idea into self-attention to give it stronger expressive power. I think that work is also very interesting. To improve attention, you either make self-attention better, or make more efficient variants, such as sparse attention or hybrid linear attention. I think these two can also be combined, because each has its own advantages and disadvantages. Sparse attention is definitely stronger at retrieval, but its drawback is that it cannot save KV cache. Linear attention can save a great deal of KV cache. I previously wrote a Zhihu answer asking why we could not combine these two approaches. For example, sparse attention could replace the global-attention layers in hybrid attention. Then we would not need the complexity of global attention, while we would still need to store KV cache; but the KV-cache size of many remaining layers could be reduced through linear attention. In terms of being efficient without performance degradation, I think that is currently my ideal efficient architecture.

items.question: Why do you think distillation helps sparse attention learn to select tokens accurately?
items.object: Learning accurate token selection in sparse attention
items.answer: I think it is the difficulty of learning. items.question: How would you make a fair comparison between sliding-window attention and linear attention?

items.answer: For a fair comparison between sliding-window attention and linear attention, I think there are two ways. One is, for example, to control their state size. Sliding window has a KV cache. Since it is a sliding window, the upper bound of that KV cache is bounded. In that case, we can treat the upper limit of its KV-cache size as the state size of sliding-window attention. Then RN has its RN state size, right? It has that number of states. If the two are roughly at the same level, I think that is a fair comparison. Because during decoding, both sliding window and RN are basically memory-bound processes. So as long as their state sizes are similar, their decoding efficiency will not differ very much. In a memory-bound setting, what mainly matters is how much state they read. As long as their states are roughly the same size, their decoding efficiency will basically be similar, because decoding is still mainly memory-bound.

items.question: How do you understand the goal of architectural innovations such as fine-grained MoE and more efficient attention?
items.object: The goals of architectural innovation through fine-grained MoE and more efficient attention
items.answer: I think these optimizations are basically reflected in this: given the same FLOPs, how can you make better use of those FLOPs and achieve a lower loss function? MoE, for example—two years ago, say around 2020 to 2023, people were all saying GPT-4 used MoE, but many places were not very quick to follow. Now MoE has basically become an established mainstream field; every company is doing this kind of fine-grained MoE. MoE can be thought of as a more efficient replacement for FFH. It can expand FFH's parameter count better while keeping its FLOPs unchanged. Then, with the same FLOPs, it can achieve a lower training loss during training. That is one point. And I think MoE may be the architectural approach with the biggest breakthrough in recent years. Then the next breakthrough point may be attention, because Transformer has two modules: an FFH and an attention. FFH has now basically been sculpted into this fine-grained-MoE form. Then I think everyone can sculpt attention as well—why not? In this way, for example, with long text, at the same FLOPs it may achieve a lower loss. I think both lines of thinking are needed: reduce FLOPs, and then, as with FFH, reducing FLOPs lets you use a larger parameter count and a larger-scale model. For example, you can stack up the total parameter count because the compute used by FFH has been reduced. Everyone knows that at large-scale training, FFH compute is dominant. Replacing it with this kind of fine-grained MoE can reduce a great deal of cost. Attention, on the other hand, does not mainly scale parameter count; what it scales is the context-window size. If its FLOPs can be brought down for long text, then long-text generation—and, for example, having many agents process many workflows and feeding them lots and lots of context—will also benefit from a larger context window.

items.question: How do you see the role of algorithm research changing as AI runs into data and compute limits?
items.object: Algorithm research under data and compute constraints
items.answer: Previously, for example, if data could keep scaling, there was not much particular use in talking about data efficiency, because everyone could just find ways to add more data, keep scaling up the model, and keep adding data. So nobody needed to touch the algorithms; everyone only needed to buy GPUs. But now, if there is a data wall and a compute wall, then in the end we may have to return to the fundamental things, namely algorithms. I think none of these things can be missing. Data, algorithms, and compute are like three horses pulling a carriage that drives the development of AI. And I remember that OpenAI's CTO also said that, at this point, the importance of algorithm research may be elevated again. If you remember that interview, I think that is what he said.

items.question: How do you assess the ceiling of the current Transformer architecture?
items.object: The limitations and future development of the Transformer architecture
items.answer: I think we should first solve the efficiency problem. Right now the efficiency problem has not been solved. It still has limitations in handling a very long context window. So everyone does a lot of context engineering and RAG, using other methods to address these problems. But if you solve the context problem, you would not need the whole RAG stack; you could put it directly into the context and do in-context RAG. As for the ceiling, first let us see whether we can get rid of global attention. That is the first point, because it really is a major bottleneck preventing the context window from continuing to scale up. I think this bottleneck will have to be removed sooner or later. The second point may be continuity. Current Transformer architectures still cannot do continuity. Then continuity, having AI learn by itself, and even—doesn't everyone want to turn pre-training into starting directly from RL, so that the model learns directly from scratch without being fed this pre-training data? These new paradigms may be what is explored next.

items.question: What do you see as the main bottleneck in scaling up and deploying linear-attention Transformers?
items.object: Infrastructure for scaling and deploying linear-attention Transformers
items.answer: I think scale-up should not present any especially big problems. Another point may be that the supporting infrastructure still needs to be built out. Flash Linear Attention only provides some Triton kernels. They are basically usable in a make-do sense, but their efficiency is certainly not optimal because they are written in Triton. So companies or others aspiring to invest in this field could perhaps spend effort optimizing these kernels. That would help continued scale-up. On the inference side, support is gradually becoming more plentiful. For example, about half a year ago I attended something like a MiniMax roundtable. The moderator was Professor Junxian, and he asked me what the main bottleneck in this field was. I said the supporting infrastructure had not kept up. He was quite surprised, because he expected me to answer something else. But that is in fact how it is. At the algorithm level, developments over the last two years already make it possible to try this at large scale. For example, Qwen 3 Next and Kimi can both be tried directly at large scale. The deployment bottleneck is probably more in the supporting infrastructure, because those two companies released those two models. The open-source community has also been quite supportive. Previously, for example, SG did not support inference for hybrid models. Now it can seize this opportunity to add inference-engine support for models such as Qwen 3 Next, MiniMax, and M1. I think this is a positive flow, a process of positive development for the field. Base-model vendors produce some promising results and release them open source. Then people building inference engines have a lot of motivation to figure out how to support these things. And when the inference support becomes better, other companies that might have felt that the inference ecosystem for Linear Transformation was too poor—that even if they could build it, deployment would be costly because the ecosystem was bad—will see that, once the ecosystem is built up, it can create a positive cycle.

items.question: How did your reading of earlier architecture papers shape your approach to developing Delta Net?
items.object: Prior architecture research and the development of Delta Net
items.answer: After applying, I had half a year of free time, and at that time I was basically researching papers on these architectures. I read many rather old papers. For example, Delta Net was originally a 2021 paper by the father of LSTM, and I remembered that work. Later, toward the end of that year, after doing Gated Linear Attention, I found that people in this field were interested in the task of in-context recall—doing retrieval from earlier text—and that immediately reminded me of a 2021 work. Because I had a very thorough grasp of the whole preceding field, I knew what angle to enter from if others in the field cared about this problem. I also knew the problems with the earlier work. For example, 2021's Delta Net did not have a guarantee of hard, hard efficiency. So later, after adding this work and working on Delta Net, I knew Delta Net was a very good model; its weakness was that people still could not use it at large scale. If I could develop an algorithm that could scale it up, that would be very meaningful work. That was roughly my chain of reasoning. And perhaps I was lucky: number three happened to yield an algorithm that could scale it up. Later, with GT and the others, I continued along that work, because we found that Detonate still could not beat Mamba Q on many tasks. Then I thought: if it cannot beat it, join it. So I took Mamba Q's gating and brought it over, and added Detonate back in. That turned A plus B into a GT Detonate.

items.question: Why do you consider revisiting neglected algorithmic techniques valuable for advancing architecture research?
items.object: Revisiting neglected algorithmic techniques
items.answer: Some good works were buried in the sea of literature because there was no follow-up. For example, Delta-Ro existed in 2021, as I said earlier, but in the following years nobody took it seriously and there was essentially no follow-up work. In terms of evolution over time, some techniques—such as fine-grained forgetting—may have existed many years ago. For example, fine-grained DK had at least a paper at IMLRP 2022. The earliest I can excavate goes back to 2016. But later, for example, Renaissance 2023 instead used a DK whose forgetting rate was at a coarse granularity. So I think previous techniques may not have been carried forward well. items.question: Why do you see Transformer as the architecture chosen by its generation of hardware?
items.object: Transformer’s hardware affinity and its advantages over LSTMs
items.answer: Transformer is certainly the chosen one. Transformer was designed at the time to run quickly on hardware. With FF, there is no need to say more: it is all large matrix multiplication, so it is fast. Before attention, people used non-parallelizable modules such as LSTM-style RNNs. LSTMs are certainly harder to accelerate on hardware. Attention has quadratic complexity—one level higher than RNNs in complexity—but it can compute the output through matrix multiplication, so its hardware affinity is much better than RNNs'. That is why people would rather use Transformer, with its higher theoretical complexity, than LSTM, with its lower theoretical complexity: their hardware-affinity performance is completely different. Algorithmic development overall needs to find algorithms with this kind of hardware affinity and better properties. Transformer attention is not only more hardware-friendly; it also truly solved some long-range dependency problems, which is why it became so popular.

items.question: What principles do you think should guide model architecture design in today’s scalability-oriented setting?
items.object: Principles for designing scalable model architectures
items.answer: Linear attention has returned to the stage today, and that also cannot be separated from this series of developments: for example, transformation algorithms that split it into chunks, and stronger designs that make more sense from a machine-learning-performance perspective. Those are the driving forces behind its development. So I strongly advocate models that are principled from a machine-learning perspective, mathematically grounded, mathematically sensible—such as Delta-Ro—and also hardware-aligned. I think model-building must be combined with current hardware. Some people say, “If I design an algorithm that is good enough, hardware companies will optimize it for me.” How could that be possible? Is your algorithm made of gold or silver, that hardware companies would optimize it for you every day? That is impossible. Your algorithm must first satisfy some very general principles. Hardware has principles, such as memory hierarchy. Matrix multiplication likewise has such principles; regardless of the hardware type, it generally follows them. There are universal principles. You may not need to optimize specifically for an H100, but I think algorithm design must at least satisfy these broadly applicable hardware principles. Otherwise, in today's scalability-oriented setting, the algorithm has basically no practical value; it is just self-amusement.

items.question: How do you think the co-evolution of hardware and Transformer should shape the next generation of model architectures?
items.object: Hardware–algorithm co-evolution and the design of future model architectures
items.answer:
At present, I think hardware evolution and Transformer have a kind of co-evolution: hardware is becoming more like what Transformer prefers. That introduces somewhat unfavorable factors for alternatives. When people build this hardware architecture, they find it is for optimizing matrix multiplication and making matrix multiplication faster and faster. Transformer contains massive amounts of matrix multiplication, so hardware wants to make fast matrix multiplication. Tensor Cores, TMI, and, recently, Blackwell's dedicated memory on the memory side for matrix multiplication are all there to optimize matrix multiplication. So perhaps people will see FlashAttention getting faster and faster—FA4 becoming faster and faster on Blackwell. Since hardware is evolving this way, from an algorithm-design perspective you must design algorithms that contain matrix multiplication, otherwise you definitely will not keep up in hardware efficiency.

One advantage of the algorithms created for Linear Attention is that they are basically matrix multiplications, though they also have some other overhead. In training they may, for example, still be less efficient than FlashAttention 4 on Blackwell, but that does not really matter: many places do not care about training efficiency; they only care about inference efficiency. So as long as it can train at a reasonable speed, prefill at a reasonable speed, and decode quickly, this kind of architecture has a market.

Also, things like fine-grained MoE and Sparse Attention reduce FLOPs while still using matrix multiplication. They definitely still need matrix multiplication, but they find ways to bring FLOPs down through algorithmic innovation, while ensuring there is a large amount of matrix multiplication. Once an algorithm is basically all matrix multiplication, hardware optimization of it is relatively quite easy, because I think hardware is moving toward ever-faster matrix multiplication. With FA4, matrix multiplication is even so fast that the exponential module becomes a bottleneck. FA4 then uses approximate methods to do that EXP. That is rather amusing: matrix multiplication is too fast. So now we should still make the best use of the fact that matrix multiplication is fast and design algorithms around it.
